opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the main reason byte-level models haven't really caught on comes down to efficiency, and that becomes clearer the more you think about scale.

When you operate directly on bytes, your sequences get a lot longer. For English text, a typical subword tokenizer compresses things by roughly a factor of four, so a byte-level model processes about four times as many positions for the same text. For other languages and scripts, especially non-Latin ones where a single character can take several bytes in UTF-8, the gap can be even larger. Since attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and every layer runs over every position, that adds up fast in both training and inference.

At small scale you can sometimes absorb that cost, and byte-level models have some really appealing properties. They don't need a fixed vocabulary, they're more robust to spelling variation, noise, and typos, and they don't have the same fairness problems that tokenizers create across languages, where some languages get chopped into many more pieces than others. But once you're training frontier-scale models, a constant-factor slowdown of four or more is a huge deal. It means more compute, more memory, slower generation, and a shorter effective context window for the same budget. So even if the byte-level model is a bit better on some robustness metric, it's very hard to justify when the tokenized model gives you so much more for the same compute.

That's really what motivated a lot of my work, including MrT5. The question was: can we keep the benefits of operating on raw bytes but recover some of the efficiency that tokenization gives us? With MrT5, we added a learned deletion mechanism early in the encoder, so the model can decide which byte representations it doesn't need to carry forward and drop them. That shortens the sequence dynamically for the rest of the network. The model learns its own compression instead of relying on a fixed, hand-designed tokenizer.

So I'd frame it this way: byte-level modeling isn't failing because it's a bad idea in principle. It's struggling because of how costs grow with scale. If we can make these models more efficient, through dynamic merging, deletion, or hierarchical architectures, then I think a lot of the advantages of tokenizer-free models become much more practical.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that byte-level models haven't caught on because, at the scales people actually train at, they just look worse on paper. If you take a transformer and you feed it raw bytes instead of subword tokens, your sequences get something like four to five times longer for English, and way more than that for a lot of other languages. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so your compute cost goes up dramatically, and you're also spending a lot of that compute on very low-information predictions, right? Predicting the next byte inside a common word is trivial. So when people run the comparison at a fixed budget, the tokenized model wins, and everyone kind of shrugs and moves on.

But I think that comparison is a little bit unfair, or at least incomplete. Tokenizers are doing a lot of hidden work for you. BPE is essentially a compression step that someone precomputed on a corpus, and it's baking in assumptions about what units of text matter. And that works great for English and for the domains that dominated the training data, and it works much less well for everything else. You get all these weird failure modes: models that can't spell, can't count letters, can't do character-level manipulation, that are brittle to typos, that tokenize some languages into way more tokens per word so they're effectively more expensive and worse for those speakers. Those aren't really modeling failures, they're tokenization failures.

So the reason I think scaling is the interesting lever is that it lets you ask a cleaner question. If the byte-level model is only losing because it's spending compute on easy predictions, then architectures that learn to allocate compute dynamically, where the model itself decides how to chunk the input rather than relying on a fixed vocabulary, should close the gap as you scale. And if the gap doesn't close, that tells you something real about the inductive biases tokenizers provide. Either way you learn something. Right now we mostly have small-scale results and a lot of folk wisdom, and I don't think folk wisdom should be the reason an entire design axis gets locked in. The field has converged really hard on one preprocessing choice, and I'd like to actually know whether that's because it's fundamentally better or just because it was convenient at the moment the recipes got fixed.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the story is that we haven’t really seen them tested at the same scale as token-based models. With bytes, you’re representing text as much longer sequences, so the model has to do more work to capture the same context. It also has to learn how those bytes compose into meaningful units, whereas a tokenizer gives you some of that structure up front.

So if a byte-level model underperforms at a smaller scale, it’s hard to know whether that’s a fundamental limitation or whether it just needs more capacity and training. Scaling could help us tease those explanations apart. But it’s an expensive experiment, and token-based models already work well, so there’s a practical reason people keep using them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that bytes make sequences much longer. A single token in a typical language model might represent a whole word or a chunk of a word, whereas at the byte level, you need several steps to represent that same text. So you’re spending more computation processing the same amount of language, and with standard attention, that longer context can get expensive very quickly.

That also makes comparisons tricky. If you give a byte-level model and a token-level model the same context length, they’re not actually seeing the same amount of text. And if you train them for the same number of steps, you may not be giving them comparable amounts of data or compute.

So I think scaling could help us understand whether there’s a fundamental limitation here, or whether byte-level models just need a different allocation of compute and a different architecture to be competitive. That uncertainty, combined with how well token-based models already work, is probably part of why they haven’t caught on.
